annotations.text:
Report UI polish — five directions against ui-polish.md.
All share the core fixes: themed edges with arrowheads and label pills, direct routes, content-sized cards, one bottom-right minimap+zoom stack, detail-level and stage dropdowns (no segmented control, no time slider, no compare/scope), docked collapsed-panel chips, full dark theming (B), panel anatomy (right).
A–C and E are built from the app's styles.css tokens; D restyles them.
The container-level board (bottom right) closes the last two walkthrough gaps: #6 interface stubs and #11 boundary containers.

Option A — Refined Float.
Keeps today's floating-cluster language: one merged top pill, details panel docked and included in fit, legend as an edge tab.
Why: smallest implementation delta.
Tradeoff: floating chrome still overlays canvas at small viewports.

Option B — Docked Workbench (dark).
Zero floating chrome: toolbar row, legend rail, tables dock. Canvas is an exact reserved rect, so fit is trivial.
Why: predictable layout; best for table-heavy work.
Tradeoff: least canvas per pixel, denser feel.

Option C — Quiet Canvas (connection selected).
One slim 44px bar; selection actions travel with the selection; panels open from docked corner chips.
Why: maximum canvas, cleanest reading.
Tradeoff: lowest discoverability; most new interaction code.
Panel anatomy is direction-independent: kv grid with one label style, connection endpoints + direction + interval, tables that auto-size and collapse empty columns. Applies to whichever option wins.

Option D — Gallery (from your IcePanel reference).
Card-first: big sans-serif names, centered card anatomy, curved connectors, calm neutral ground, chrome reduced to a top bar + left view rail.
Why: the calmest, most product-like read; typography does the hierarchy work.
Tradeoff: biggest departure from the current mono-technical identity; larger cards mean fewer nodes per screen.

Option D applied to the report's existing dependency view (three-column focus layout in styles.css today): focus selector, incoming/outgoing columns, connection-count pills on curved fan-out edges. Pairs with any of A–C as the dependency screen.

Option E — Consolidated Docks. The draw.io/Lucid zoning model: scope determines placement.
Top bar = global only (file, search ⌘K, theme). Left dock = ALL document/view state in one palette (views, detail level, stage, tags). Right inspector = everything about the current selection, always in the same place. Canvas floats exactly two things: the nav cluster and a selection toolbar.
Why: one home per function — nothing is ever 'somewhere else'.
Tradeoff: two permanent docks cost ~540px of width; least immersive of the five.

Diagramming-tool best practices baked into E (draw.io, Lucidchart, Miro, Figma conventions):
1. Scope determines placement — global → top bar; document/view → left dock; selection → right inspector.
2. One palette, not scattered clusters; panels dock and reserve layout space, never overlay content, and collapse to stable edge strips.
3. Selection actions live in a contextual toolbar at the selection (Lucid/Miro) — never spliced into global bars (ui-polish #16).
4. One navigation cluster bottom-right: fit, zoom, minimap.
5. ⌘K command palette as the consolidator for everything else searchable (jump to entity, run action).
6. Progressive disclosure: rare controls inside panels, not top-level chrome.
A and C already follow 3–4; E applies all six.

Container level, done readably (issues #6 and #11): the boundary gets a fill tint, a labeled header with container count, and a collapse control; containers inside are content-sized cards; interfaces render as glyph stubs ATTACHED to the boundary where each edge crosses, with technology labels — never as detached empty boxes. Direction-independent, shown here in the A/E token family.
